newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O.Licht - 2nd Estimate of world coffee balance.
newsitem.headline: F.O.Licht - 2nd Estimate of world coffee balance.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.
SECOND ESTIMATE OF WORLD COFFEE BALANCE 1996/97

There can be no doubt that the very high levels to which world coffee prices have soared in recent months will have had a depressing effect upon consumption. The question is: by how much? There is no easy answer; the amount of publicity about rising prices has led both retailers and consumers to increase their inventories. Consequently the immediate effect of the higher prices may be an apparent increase in consumption rather than the reverse. As the year progresses, however, the picture should become clearer. Though the reaction to the steep rises may be lagged, industry sources throughout Europe and the USA fear coffee sales will fall.

Roasters in Germany believe current prices could bring a fall in consumption of three to five per cent while coffee experts in France expect a drop following April price increases. In Italy there has been a pronounced switching to lower quality blends. Price elasticity in Eastern Europe is greater than in the West and if prices are maintained at their current levels imports must be expected to be hit. So far demand in the USA has been fairly stable, which probably reflects the booming economy, though it has been suggested that consumption in the calendar year might fall by as much as 1 million bags. Total consumption in importing countries in 1996/97 is estimated at 74.5 million bags to which has to be added about 25 million bags in producing countries, making a total of 99.5 million bags. For calendar year 1997 consumption in importing countries is expected to be about 1.5 million bags lower.

Production in 1996/97 is now forecast at 99 million bags, 11.1 million bags up on the year, and 1.3 million bags up from our first forecast. Nevertheless, there has been an important change. The estimate for robusta coffee has been raised by 1.2 million bags while the figure for arabica has been reduced slightly by 42,000 bags. This underlines the current market trend which indicates a scarcity of arabica and more than adequate supplies of robusta.

Total production in Africa is now put at 19.2 million bags, up from 17.5 million bags the previous year. Robustas are accounting for an increasing share with arabica more or less unchanged. The Cote d'Ivoire is the largest producer in Africa with output estimated at 4-5 million bags. The upper end of the range is probably unrealistic at present but the government is endeavouring to encourage an increase in production for export. At 19.0 million bags estimated output in North and Central America is higher than was anticipated earlier, though that figure is still down from the 19.2 million bags produced last season. Mexico is the largest grower in the region though the estimated 5.2 million bags is 250,000 bags below the previous season's figure, which reflects the biannual production cycle as well as frosts in December 1996. The government has added coffee to the nine basic commodities which qualify for the national agriculture support programme. The South American scene is dominated by Brazil where production in 1996/97 is expected to rise to 28.5 million bags, up from the previous season's drought and frost damaged 15.8 million bags. Estimates of output in Colombia vary widely but all of them are well below last season's 12.9 million bags. The total output in South America is put at 42.7 million bags compared with 33.6 million bags the previous season. Output in Asia is forecast at 17.1 million bags or 4 per cent more than in 1995/96. Indonesian output of 6.5 million bags was slightly up on the year. Poor weather conditions are expected to lead to a fall in 1997/98. Output in Oceania is largely based in Papua New Guinea, where about 1 million bags is expected.

Stocks in importing countries are now at twenty year lows. Producer stocks are difficult to assess but they are also now at the lowest level for years. Consequently there is little leeway in case there should be a production shortfall in 1997/98. Looking at the overall production figures for 1997/98 and assuming no major shortfalls total indicated production might be sufficient to meet market requirements. However it is still far too early in the season to be precise about next season's crop and the only conclusion which can be drawn at present is that even without a frost in Brazil the market will remain in a highly precarious state due to the low level of mainly high quality stocks. Excessive prices cannot be in the longer term interest of producers and they should do all they can to maximise production so as to avert shortages which can only lead to long term loss of market for coffee and a long period of low prices.
